comparison: Both strongly support the genetic strategy's specificity and comprehensiveness for labeling AACs. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative validation (>97% specificity across regions C31, C42, C50) and convergence of two intersectional approaches (C23, C28). Peer reviewers affirm the approach is rigorous and convincing, with Reviewer 2 noting it identifies AACs 'specifically and, apparently, nearly completely.' Both treat this as a major methodological achievement.

Complete agreement on the expanded brain-wide distribution of AACs. Both evaluations cite the comprehensive whole-brain imaging methodology (C15) and accept the distribution across cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, and other regions (C16-C20, C22). OpenEval notes C82 is appropriately stated as hypothesis with incomplete validation in some regions. Peer reviewers unanimously treat this as a major, convincing discovery.

Both support the quantitative density measurements and morphological characterizations. OpenEval emphasizes the automated detection methodology (C32) and statistical analysis of regional/laminar distributions (C33-C37). Peer reviewers accept these detailed anatomical findings without critique, with Reviewer 2 noting they provide 'a roadmap for subsequent, detailed studies.' Both also reference morphological diversity (C5, C6, C38, C40, C41).

Both support the hippocampal findings including CA2 enrichment. OpenEval focuses on quantitative density measurements (C43-C44) and notes the inference about differential innervation (C45) is reasonable but based on an assumption. Peer reviewers accept the surprising CA2 enrichment and high validation rate (98.2% from C42) as convincing, without challenging the quantitative claims.

Divergence in confidence level. OpenEval supports amygdala/claustrum AAC findings (C46-C53) based on immunohistochemistry validation (97.2% specificity C50) and appropriate methodology, noting C54 speculation is appropriately labeled. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 3's concerns about inconsistent pAAC definitions between methods and text, though the overall presence in these regions is not disputed.

Both support the novel finding of AACs in olfactory structures. OpenEval emphasizes dense labeling, whole-brain imaging (C56, C58), and morphological validation (C57, C60). Peer reviewers explicitly state the evidence for pAACs in 'several olfactory centers' is 'convincing' and treat this as an important discovery where AACs were not previously recognized.

Both support lateral septum AAC findings (C60). OpenEval notes morphological similarity to neocortical AACs. Peer reviewers include lateral septum in their statement about convincing evidence for pAACs in novel brain regions. Complete agreement on this discovery.

Perfect claim overlap (C61-C66) with both supporting cortical AAC input tracing. OpenEval details the intersectional tTA2/rabies methodology, quantitative analysis, and linear correlation validation (r=0.8874), noting Pvalb comparison complications. Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly states the rabies tracing 'supports the utility of this novel genetic approach' for revealing input patterns.

Perfect claim overlap (C67-C69) with both supporting hippocampal AAC input findings. OpenEval emphasizes the characterization of input cell types using immunohistochemistry/HCR RNA-FISH and notes contrast with CA3 AACs (C88). Peer reviewers accept these connectivity findings as supporting the genetic strategy's utility without challenge.

Perfect claim overlap (C70-C72) with both supporting BLA AAC input tracing. OpenEval notes this represents the first comprehensive mapping of BLA AAC inputs with characterization of neurotransmitter phenotypes (C72). Peer Reviewer 3 includes BLA in the statement that rabies tracing reveals region-specific and common inputs, supporting the genetic approach.

Significant divergence. OpenEval supports the comparative analysis between Unc5b and Pthlh intersectional strategies (C24-C26, C29-C30), noting thorough characterization including off-target labeling identification. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN with Reviewer 2 raising concerns about Pthlh;Nkx2.1 being 'less convincing,' noting 'distinct differences' and suggesting the comparison 'detracts from the otherwise convincing argument.'

Both support the neocortical validation data (C31: 97.3% specificity). OpenEval includes this as part of comprehensive multi-region validation. Peer reviewers specifically note the validation 'near markers of axon initial segments' provides support for AAC identity and method specificity. Complete agreement on this quantitative validation.

Both support morphological diversity findings. OpenEval emphasizes sparse single-cell labeling methodology (C6, C38, C40) for characterizing translaminar subtypes, noting C39 functional speculation is appropriately labeled. Peer reviewers accept morphological characterizations without critique as part of the broader anatomical analysis.

Both support cartridge density mapping across brain regions. OpenEval details the synaptophysin-EGFP reporter methodology (C41) and normalized density measurements (C59). Peer reviewers accept this finding, with only minimal claim overlap (C59) but no disagreement on the quantitative regional comparisons.

Both address speculative/interpretive claims but with different emphasis. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting these represent future directions and interpretations (C73, C78, C80-C86, C96) rather than directly tested results. Peer reviewers support the broader implications (C1, C2, C73, C82-C85), stating findings will lead to new insights and the work provides important tools, treating implications as well-supported.

Partial overlap on nomenclature and conceptual framework (C1, C2). OpenEval supports these as established nomenclature and defining characteristics. Peer reviewers accept the conceptual framework and broader significance, emphasizing the work will be 'of broad interest' and lead to new insights.

OpenEval evaluates claims about prior work and field context (C9-C12, C74) as supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific background/context claims.

OpenEval evaluates numerous citations of prior work (C7, C8, C21, C75-C77, C79, C87, C88, C90, C91) as accurate and providing appropriate context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific literature citations.
